lessons.title: Inversion for emphasis
lessons.summary: Use formal inverted structures after negative adverbs.

sections.title: Inversion for emphasis
sections.body_md:
After some negative or limiting adverbs at the start of a sentence, use question word order:

- *Never **have I** seen such a result.*
- *Rarely **do** students finish early.*
- *Not only **did** prices rise, but wages also fell.*
- *Only after the test **did we** realise the mistake.*
- *No sooner **had** we arrived than it started to rain.*

sections.title: Examples
sections.body_md:
- ***Seldom has** a policy been so popular.*
- ***Under no circumstances should** you share your password.*

lessons.title: Cleft sentences
lessons.summary: Focus attention on one part of a sentence.

sections.title: Cleft sentences
sections.body_md:
**Cleft sentences** split a sentence to emphasise one part:

- ***It was** the cost **that** worried people.* (not the design)
- ***What** surprised me **was** the speed.*
- ***The reason why** they left **was** the noise.*
- ***All** we need **is** more time.*

sections.title: Examples
sections.body_md:
- *It is the students **who** benefit most.*
- *What the data shows is a clear rise in demand.*

sections.title: Participle clauses
sections.body_md:
Participle clauses replace a full clause when the subject is the same:

- **Present participle (-ing)** for active or simultaneous actions: ***Walking** home, I saw an accident.*
- **Past participle** for passive meaning: ***Built** in 1900, the hall needs repairs.*
- **Having + past participle** for an earlier action: ***Having finished** the report, she left.*

The subject must be the same in both parts, or the sentence becomes confusing.

sections.title: Examples
sections.body_md:
- ***Funded** by the council, the project began in May.*
- ***Having analysed** the data, the team published the results.*

lessons.title: Mixed conditionals
lessons.summary: Link a past condition to a present result, and the reverse.

sections.title: Mixed conditionals
sections.body_md:
- **Past condition → present result:** *If* + past perfect, *would* + verb. *If I **had studied** medicine, I **would be** a doctor now.*
- **Present condition → past result:** *If* + past simple, *would have* + past participle. *If she **were** more careful, she **wouldn't have made** that mistake.*

sections.title: Examples
sections.body_md:
- *If they **had invested** earlier, they **would be** richer today.*
- *If I **didn't** trust him, I **wouldn't have lent** him money.*

lessons.title: Nominalisation
lessons.summary: Turn verbs and adjectives into nouns for a formal style.

sections.title: Nominalisation
sections.body_md:
Academic writing often uses **nouns** instead of verbs: this is **nominalisation**.

- *Prices increased* → ***The increase in prices** ...*
- *They analysed the data* → ***Analysis of the data** showed ...*
- *People are aware* → ***Public awareness** ...*

It makes writing more compact and objective. Do not overuse it: clarity matters most.

sections.title: Examples
sections.body_md: - *The **introduction of** the new law led to **a reduction in** accidents.*

lessons.title: Cohesion: reference words
lessons.summary: Link sentences with this, these, such, the former and the latter.

sections.title: Cohesion: reference words
sections.body_md:
Reference words point back to ideas you already mentioned, so you do not repeat them:

- *this / these + noun*: *Costs rose. **This increase** worried firms.*
- *such + noun*: ***Such** changes take time.*
- *the former / the latter*: first and second of two things.
- *it / they / them* must clearly refer to one noun.

sections.title: Examples
sections.body_md: - *Bikes and buses both reduce traffic. **The former** is cheaper; **the latter** carries more people.*

lessons.title: Formal and informal register
lessons.summary: Choose the right tone for academic writing and for spoken situations.

sections.title: Formal and informal register
sections.body_md:
**Academic writing** is formal: no contractions (*do not*, not *don't*), no slang, few phrasal verbs, precise words.

| Informal | Formal |
|---|---|
| get | obtain, receive |
| look into | investigate |
| lots of | a large number of / considerable |
| kids | children |
| really big | substantial |

In speaking tasks such as Respond to a Situation, match the person: polite with a manager or teacher, friendly with a friend.

sections.title: Examples
sections.body_md:
- Informal: *Lots of kids don't get enough sleep.*
- Formal: *A large number of children do not receive sufficient sleep.*

lessons.title: Concise writing
lessons.summary: Say more with fewer words, which helps with word limits.

sections.title: Concise writing
sections.body_md:
Cut words that add nothing:

- *due to the fact that* → *because*
- *in order to* → *to*
- *at this point in time* → *now*
- *a large number of* → *many*
- *it is important to note that* → (often delete)

This helps in Summarize Written Text (one sentence, up to 75 words) and Summarize Spoken Text (50–70 words).

sections.title: Examples
sections.body_md:
- Wordy: *Due to the fact that it was raining, the match was cancelled.*
- Concise: *The match was cancelled because of rain.*

lessons.title: Making inferences
lessons.summary: Understand what a writer or speaker means but does not say directly.

sections.title: Making inferences
sections.body_md:
An **inference** is a logical conclusion from the text. It must be **supported** by the text, not by your own opinion.

- Look for clues: word choice, examples, contrasts.
- Ask: *What must be true if this is true?*
- Avoid options that go too far (*always, never, all*).

sections.title: Examples
sections.body_md: *"The new café is always full, even on weekdays."* → Inference: *The café is popular.* (Not: *It is the best café in town.*)

lessons.title: Writer's purpose and tone
lessons.summary: Recognise why a text was written and the writer's attitude.

sections.title: Writer's purpose and tone
sections.body_md:
**Purpose:** to inform, explain, persuade, compare, warn, describe a process.

**Tone:** neutral, critical, enthusiastic, cautious, concerned.

Clues: strong adjectives (*alarming, impressive*), modal verbs (*must, should*), hedging (*may, might*).

sections.title: Examples
sections.body_md: - *"Cities **must** act now to prevent an **alarming** rise in heat deaths."* → purpose: persuade; tone: concerned.

lessons.title: Signposting in lectures
lessons.summary: Follow the structure of a talk from the speaker's signals.

sections.title: Signposting in lectures
sections.body_md:
Speakers use **signposts** to show where the talk is going:

- Starting: *Today I'd like to talk about ..., First of all ...*
- Adding: *Another point is ..., Moreover ...*
- Contrasting: *On the other hand ..., However ...*
- Example: *To illustrate this ..., Take ... for example.*
- Concluding: *To sum up ..., So, the key point is ...*

Note what comes after a signpost: it is often a main point you need for Retell Lecture or Summarize Spoken Text.

sections.title: Examples
sections.body_md: *"**To sum up**, small daily changes have a bigger effect than one big change."* → the conclusion.

lessons.title: Fact and opinion
lessons.summary: Tell the difference between what is proven and what someone believes.

sections.title: Fact and opinion
sections.body_md:
- A **fact** can be checked: *The bridge opened in 1932.*
- An **opinion** shows a belief or judgement: *It is the most beautiful bridge in the world.*

Opinion signals: *I think, in my view, should, best, worst, beautiful, unfortunately*. In multiple-choice tasks, choose what the text **states**, not what you believe.

sections.title: Examples
sections.body_md:
- Fact: *Sales fell by 10% in 2023.*
- Opinion: *The new design was a terrible idea.*
